_about: Third-party pairs worth a referee page (docs/seo.md, Phase 2b). Only pairs that share an audience. The canonical order is the one people search: the less famous product first, the way somebody types it when they know the smaller tool and want to know how it compares. The reverse 301s to it (site/_redirects). thirdOption is opt-in: Vibresia appears on a pair's page only when it is true, and a test fails if it shows anywhere else.

pairs.audience: MilkDrop fans deciding between the original Winamp plug-in and its open-source rebuild.
pairs.whyCompared: projectM is a reimplementation of MilkDrop that plays the same presets, so people who remember MilkDrop look at both.
pairs.thirdOptionWhy: Neither is a finished Mac app that hears every app's audio: MilkDrop doesn't run on a Mac, and projectM's Mac apps are previews.

pairs.audience: Windows users who want MilkDrop-style visuals, for watching or for VJing.
pairs.whyCompared: NestDrop is built on the MilkDrop engine and plays its presets, adding VJ controls and video output.

pairs.audience: VJs choosing their main live-video software, on a Mac or across Mac and Windows.
pairs.whyCompared: Both are full VJ applications used for live shows, and on a Mac they are the two most common choices.

pairs.audience: Visual artists deciding between a ready-made VJ application and a programming environment for live visuals.
pairs.whyCompared: They're different kinds of tool, but both are used for live visuals, and people starting out often weigh one against the other.

pairs.audience: Mac-based visual artists choosing between a node-based environment and a modular VJ application.
pairs.whyCompared: Both run on a Mac and both can build a live visual show, from different starting points.

pairs.audience: Mac and Windows VJs choosing between the two VJ applications people compare most.
pairs.whyCompared: Both are VJ applications for putting video on screens and projectors at a show, and they are the pair people weigh up when they are looking for one.

pairs.audience: People setting up a live video feed, choosing between a VJ application and free streaming software.
pairs.whyCompared: Both put video on a screen live, one as a paid VJ rig and one as free recording and streaming software, and people building a show weigh one against the other.

pairs.audience: Venue and installation teams choosing media-server software for a live show.
pairs.whyCompared: Both drive screens and projectors with prepared media at a show, and the people booked to run that show are the ones who compare them.

pairs.audience: Creative coders and 3D artists choosing a tool for live visuals and installation work.
pairs.whyCompared: Both build visuals from nodes and scripts and both are free to start with, so people starting out in either often weigh one against the other.

pairs.audience: Mac and Windows artists building live visuals from a patch of nodes.
pairs.whyCompared: Both are real-time visual programming environments with a patch of nodes and a live renderer, and both run on a Mac, so they get compared directly.

pairs.audience: People running a live video feed, choosing between paid production software and free streaming software.
pairs.whyCompared: Both switch between sources and send the result out as a stream or a recording, and one of them is free, so people setting up a stream weigh one against the other.

pairs.audience: People running a live show or a live stream, choosing between a production switcher and a VJ application.
pairs.whyCompared: Both take video sources and put them on a screen live, and both are paid, so people doing either job weigh one against the other.

pairs.audience: People streaming an event, choosing between two paid live production tools.
pairs.whyCompared: Both are live video production software for streaming and recording, and they are the pair people compare once they are past the free option.

pairs.audience: Venue and installation teams driving screens and projectors with prepared media.
pairs.whyCompared: Both play prepared media to screens at an event, from different starting points: one a media server with a timeline, one a VJ application you perform from.

pairs.audience: People running a show with prepared media, whether a concert or a theatre production.
pairs.whyCompared: Both cue media for a live show, one from a show-control timeline and one from a VJ application, and the people booking the show are the ones who compare them.

pairs.audience: Churches and live events running video on a stage screen.
pairs.whyCompared: Both put video on a stage screen at an event, and the tech teams running churches and venues are the ones weighing one against the other.

pairs.audience: People streaming or recording an event, choosing between paid and free software.
pairs.whyCompared: Both mix sources and output a finished feed, and one of them is free, so the choice is often between price and features.

pairs.audience: People running a live event who need a video feed out.
pairs.whyCompared: Both switch between sources and output a live feed, and both are paid, so people setting up an event weigh one against the other.

pairs.audience: Creative coders building visuals for installations and live work.
pairs.whyCompared: Both build visuals procedurally and both are node-based, so people starting in either often weigh one against the other.

pairs.audience: Visual artists building live visuals on a Mac.
pairs.whyCompared: Both build a visual system and run it live, one as a node graph and one as mapped surfaces, cues and fixtures.

pairs.audience: Artists mapping video onto surfaces and driving lighting at live events.
pairs.whyCompared: Both warp video onto real surfaces and both control fixtures, and they are the two tools people compare for installation work.
